title: Spreadsheet Skills for Study and Work
summary: Learn the cells, formulas, lookups, charts and habits you need to build reliable sheets in Excel or Google Sheets.
audience: Students who need Excel or Google Sheets for school, university or work

body.p: A spreadsheet is a grid. Columns are labelled with letters (A, B, C), rows with numbers (1, 2, 3), and each box where they meet is a cell. The cell in column B and row 3 is called B3. This name is the cell reference, and formulas use it to find data. Excel and Google Sheets work in almost the same way, so everything in this course applies to both unless a note says otherwise.

A range is a block of neighbouring cells, written with a colon between the first and last cell. B2:B6 means the five cells from B2 down to B6, and B2:D6 means the rectangle three columns wide and five rows tall. Below is a small marks table that we will use throughout the course. Row 1 holds headings and rows 2 to 6 hold data.

body.code:
A         B      C        D
1  Student    Maths  English  Science
2  Amina        72      65       58
3  Kwame        81      70       64
4  Fatmata      55      48       62
5  Lamin        90      77       85
6  Wanjiru      43      60       51

list: Click a cell and type. Press Enter to confirm and move down, or Tab to move right.
Numbers align to the right and text aligns to the left by default. If a number sits on the left, it was probably entered as text.
Keep one kind of data in each column and put headings in the first row. This makes sorting, filtering and charts work properly.
Never leave blank rows inside a table, because many tools treat a blank row as the end of the data.

body.p: Every formula starts with an equals sign. If you type =5+3 in a cell and press Enter, the cell shows 8. A formula that refers to other cells updates automatically when those cells change, which is the main reason spreadsheets are so useful. The fill handle, the small square at the bottom right of a selected cell, copies a formula down or across when you drag it.

body.tip: Spain and some other countries use a version of Excel where function names are translated, for example SUMA for SUM, and arguments are separated with semicolons instead of commas. This course writes formulas in the English form with commas, which Google Sheets in English also uses.

lessons.title: Core formulas: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, ROUND

body.p: Functions are ready-made formulas. You give them a range and they return a result. For the Maths marks in B2:B6 (72, 81, 55, 90 and 43), these are the most common ones.

list: =SUM(B2:B6) adds the values: 72 + 81 + 55 + 90 + 43 = 341.
=AVERAGE(C2:C6) gives the mean of the English marks 65, 70, 48, 77 and 60: 320 divided by 5 = 64.
=MAX(D2:D6) returns the largest Science mark, 85, and =MIN(D2:D6) returns the smallest, 51.
=COUNT(B2:B6) returns 5, because COUNT counts only the cells that contain numbers. Use COUNTA to count non-empty cells of any kind.

body.p: Now add three columns to the right. In E2 we total each student's marks, and in F2 we find the average. Type the formula in row 2 and drag the fill handle down to row 6.

list: E2: =SUM(B2:D2)
F2: =ROUND(AVERAGE(B2:D2),1)

body.p: The results are shown below. For Kwame, 81 + 70 + 64 = 215, and 215 divided by 3 is 71.666..., which ROUND shows as 71.7.

ROUND(number, digits) rounds a value to the number of decimal places you choose. With 1234.567: =ROUND(1234.567,1) gives 1234.6, =ROUND(1234.567,0) gives 1235, and a negative number rounds to the left of the decimal point, so =ROUND(1234.567,-2) gives 1200. Both Excel and Google Sheets round halves away from zero, so =ROUND(2.5,0) is 3.

body.tip: The same formulas work in Excel and Google Sheets. In both, you can select a range with the mouse while typing a formula, instead of typing the cell names.

lessons.title: Decisions and conditional totals: IF, COUNTIF, SUMIF

body.p: The IF function chooses between two results. Its form is IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false). Suppose the pass mark is 55 and the averages are in F2:F6. In G2 we type the formula below and copy it down.
Text inside a formula must be in straight double quotation marks. Fatmata's average is exactly 55.0, which meets the test F>=55, so she passes; Wanjiru's 51.3 does not.

body.code:
F       G
1  Average  Result
2    65.0  Pass
3    71.7  Pass
4    55.0  Pass
5    84.0  Pass
6    51.3  Resit

body.p: COUNTIF(range, condition) counts the cells that meet a condition. =COUNTIF(G2:G6,"Pass") returns 4 because four students passed. =COUNTIF(B2:B6,">=60") returns 3, since the Maths marks 72, 81 and 90 are at least 60. Notice that a comparison such as >=60 goes inside quotation marks.
SUMIF(range, condition, sum_range) adds only the matching rows. Here is a class trip budget in Kenyan shillings.

body.code:
A                    B          C
1  Item                 Category   Amount (KES)
2  Bus hire             Transport   12000
3  Lunch packs          Food         8500
4  Entry tickets        Tickets      6000
5  Water                Food         1500
6  Return fuel top-up   Transport    3500
7  Printing             Admin         800

list: =SUMIF(B2:B7,"Food",C2:C7) returns 10000, from 8500 + 1500.
=SUMIF(B2:B7,"Transport",C2:C7) returns 15500, from 12000 + 3500.
=COUNTIF(B2:B7,"Food") returns 2, the number of food rows.

body.tip: Conditions are not case sensitive, so "food" and "Food" match the same cells. Excel and Google Sheets both support these three functions in the same form.

body.p: A lookup finds a value in a table using a key. Below is a price list in Ghana cedis in A1:B5, with headings in row 1.

body.code:
A           B
1  Product     Price (GHS)
2  Notebook         12
3  Pen                 3
4  Ruler               5
5  Calculator         85

body.p: =VLOOKUP("Ruler",A2:B5,2,FALSE) searches the first column of A2:B5 for Ruler and returns the value from column 2 of that range, which is 5. FALSE means exact match, which you should use for names and codes. VLOOKUP works in every version of Excel and in Google Sheets. XLOOKUP is newer: =XLOOKUP("Ruler",A2:A5,B2:B5) also returns 5. XLOOKUP is available in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and later, and Google Sheets, but not in Excel 2016 or 2019, so use VLOOKUP if you are unsure.

With TRUE (approximate match), VLOOKUP finds the largest key that is not above your value, and the first column must be sorted in ascending order. This is ideal for grade bands. Put 0, 50, 60 and 70 in I2:I5 with the grades F, C, B and A in J2:J5. Then =VLOOKUP(58,$I$2:$J$5,2,TRUE) returns C, because 58 sits between 50 and 60. An average of 71.7 returns A.

When you copy a formula, normal references shift with it. This is called relative referencing. A dollar sign locks a reference: $B$1 always points to B1 wherever you copy the formula. Imagine a UK shop with the VAT rate 0.2 (20 percent) in B1 and net prices in pounds in B4:B6.

body.code:
A          B        C
1  VAT rate   0.2
3  Item       Net GBP  Gross GBP
4  Book       15.00    18.000
5  Bag        24.00    28.800
6  Pen pack    4.50    5.400

body.p: In C4 type =B4*(1+$B$1) and copy it down. In C5 it becomes =B5*(1+$B$1): B4 changed to B5, but $B$1 stayed. The results are 15.00 x 1.2 = 18.00, 24.00 x 1.2 = 28.80 and 4.50 x 1.2 = 5.40. Without the dollar signs, C5 would point to B2, which is empty, and the answer would be wrong.

A mixed reference locks only the row or the column. In a times table, put 2, 3, 4 in B1:D1 and 5, 6, 7 in A2:A4, then type =$A2*B$1 in B2 and copy across and down. $A locks the column and B$1 locks the row. The cell D4 then holds =$A4*D$1, which is 7 x 4 = 28.

body.tip: Press F4 in Excel while the cursor is on a reference to cycle through $B$1, B$1, $B1 and B1. In Google Sheets, type the dollar signs yourself.

lessons.title: Formatting, sorting, filtering and a simple chart

body.p: Good formatting makes a sheet readable without changing its values. Select cells and choose a number format such as currency, percent or number with fixed decimals. A cell holding 0.2 can be shown as 20%, and 12000 can be shown as KES 12,000 or with thousands separators. Formatting changes only what you see. If a cell holds 71.6667 and is formatted to show one decimal place, it displays 71.7 but still stores 71.6667, and later formulas use the full value. Use ROUND when you need the stored value itself to change.

list: Make the heading row bold and give it a fill colour so it stands out.
Widen columns by double-clicking the border between column letters.
Freeze the top row (View, Freeze) so headings stay visible while scrolling.
Use the same number of decimals in a column.

body.p: Sorting reorders rows. Select one cell inside the table, then use Data, Sort and choose the column and the direction. Sorting the marks table by Maths from largest to smallest gives: Lamin 90, Kwame 81, Amina 72, Fatmata 55, Wanjiru 43. Always sort the whole table. If you select only one column, the other columns stay in place and the rows no longer match.

Filtering hides rows that do not meet a condition without deleting them. Turn on Data, Filter, open the arrow on the Maths heading and choose a number filter, such as greater than or equal to 60. Only Amina, Kwame and Lamin remain visible; the other rows are hidden, not removed. Clear the filter to see everything again. Filter works in the same way in Excel and Google Sheets, though Sheets has a Filter views option for sharing.

steps: Select the cells that hold the labels and the numbers, for example the category names and the totals.
Choose Insert, then Chart (Sheets) or Insert, then a chart type (Excel).
Pick a column chart to compare amounts across categories.
Add a clear title and label the axes, for example Cost in KES.
Check that the bars match the numbers in the table.

body.p: For the trip budget, the category totals are Transport 15500, Food 10000, Tickets 6000 and Admin 800 shillings. A column chart makes it easy to see that transport is the largest cost. Use a line chart for change over time, and use a pie chart only when you show parts of one whole with a few slices.

Now combine everything into a class trip budget. The table from lesson 3 sits in A1:C7, with the amounts in C2:C7. Below it we add a summary in column C, with labels in column B. Build it step by step.

body.code:
Cell  Label              Entry                   Result
C8    Total cost         =SUM(C2:C7)             32300
C9    Students           20 (typed)              20
C10   Cost per student   =ROUND(C8/C9,0)         1615
C11   Fee charged        1700 (typed)            1700
C12   Collected          =C9*C11                 34000
C13   Surplus            =C12-C8                 1700
C14   Status             =IF(C13>=0,"Funded","Short")  Funded

body.p: The six costs add up to 32300 shillings. Divided among 20 students that is exactly 1615 each, so a fee of 1700 covers it. Collecting 20 x 1700 = 34000 leaves a surplus of 1700. Because the surplus is not below zero, the status is Funded. Change the number of students or the fee and watch every result update.

Add a share column to see where money goes. In D2 type =C2/$C$8 and copy it down, then format column D as percent. The absolute reference keeps the total fixed. For the whole Food category, =SUMIF(B2:B7,"Food",C2:C7)/C8 equals 10000 divided by 32300, which is about 31.0 percent.

list: Heading row is bold, amounts use one number format.
Typed inputs such as students and fee are in their own labelled cells, so you never edit a formula to change them.
Totals use ranges, not a list of typed numbers.
A chart shows the category totals with a title and labelled axes.
You have tested the sheet by changing an input and checking the answer by hand.

body.p: To practise, repeat the project as a marks sheet: use the table from lesson 1, add Total and Average columns, an IF column for Pass or Resit, a grade lookup, and a chart of the averages. Those are the same skills in a different setting. If you use Excel with a language other than English, remember to translate function names and use your list separator.

body.tip: Save copies of your work with clear names such as class-trip-budget-v1. Google Sheets saves automatically; in Excel, press Ctrl+S often.
